title: Adding, Subtracting and Multiplying Fractions
bigQuestion: How do you combine, take away or scale amounts when those amounts are fractions?

story.title: Twice the Pancakes
story.kicker: A Saturday breakfast for eight people turns a simple recipe into a puzzle about fourths, halves and cups.
paragraphs: Jonah's dad makes pancakes every Saturday from a card that serves 4 people. Today two cousins and their parents are coming, so 8 people will eat. "Double everything," Dad says, and hands Jonah the card. The first line reads: 3/4 cup of milk.

Jonah thinks out loud. "Two times 3/4. That is 3/4 plus 3/4." He adds the tops and gets 6. Then he adds the bottoms and gets 8. "Six eighths," he says, and reaches for the measuring cup. Dad stops him. "Is 6/8 more than one cup or less?" Jonah looks at the cup. The 6/8 line sits below the 1-cup line.

That cannot be right. One 3/4 cup of milk is already most of a cup, and Jonah needs two of them. Two of something has to be more than one of it. He tries again, this time keeping the fourths as fourths: 3 fourths plus 3 fourths is 6 fourths. Four fourths make a cup, so 6 fourths is 1 cup and 2/4 more. That is 1 1/2 cups. The cup line agrees.

The flour line says 1 1/2 cups. Doubled, that is 3 cups. Then Jonah finds the problem cooks know well: the 1-cup scoop is in the dishwasher, and only the 1/2-cup scoop is clean. He has to figure out how many half-cup scoops make 3 cups. He counts by halves and gets 6 scoops.

By the time the batter is mixed, Jonah has added fractions, doubled a mixed number and counted halves into wholes. He also learned why his first answer was wrong. This chapter walks through each of those moves so you can trust your answer before you pour.
story.think: Jonah's first answer was 6/8 cup. How could he tell, without measuring, that it had to be wrong?

lessons.title: Adding With Like Denominators
lessons.mainIdea: When denominators match, add the numerators and keep the denominator, because you are counting pieces of the same size.
reading: Ava eats 3/8 of a pizza and Ben eats 2/8. How much did they eat together? The slices are all eighths, the same size. Three eighths plus two eighths is five eighths, the same way 3 apples plus 2 apples is 5 apples. So 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8. Fractions with *like denominators* add by counting the numerators. The denominator does not change.

A number line shows the *sum*. Start at 3/8 and jump 2 more eighths to land on 5/8. Sometimes the sum passes 1. Try 5/6 + 4/6. Five sixths plus four sixths is nine sixths, or 9/6. Six sixths make 1 whole, and 3 sixths are left. So 9/6 = 1 3/6, which is 1 1/2.

The most common mistake is adding the denominators too: 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/16. Here is why that is wrong. 5/16 is smaller than 3/8, because 3/8 = 6/16. Adding more pizza cannot leave you with less pizza. The denominator names the size of the pieces, and the piece size does not change when you add more pieces.

words.d: the same denominator in two or more fractions, like 3/8 and 2/8
the answer to an addition problem; the sum of 3/8 and 2/8 is 5/8

look.title: Pizza Night Leftovers
look.text: Two boxes hold leftover pizza. Each pizza was cut into 8 equal slices. The first box has 3 slices left and the second has 4 slices left. Marcus wants to know how much pizza is left in all. Later, a third box turns up with 6 slices, and he adds 5/8 + 6/8.
look.prompt: What fraction of a pizza is in the first two boxes together? When Marcus adds 5/8 + 6/8, how many whole pizzas does he have, and how much is left over?

check.why: Two fifths plus two fifths is four fifths. Add the numerators, 2 + 2 = 4, and keep the denominator 5.
5 + 3 = 8 sixths, or 8/6. Six sixths make 1, and 2/6 = 1/3 is left, so the sum is 1 1/3.

check.q: A student writes 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/16. Why is that wrong?
choices: because 5/16 is smaller than 3/8, and adding more cannot give less
check.why: 3/8 equals 6/16, so 5/16 is less than what Ava ate alone. The pieces stay eighths; the sum is 5/8.

lessons.title: Subtracting With Like Denominators
lessons.mainIdea: When denominators match, subtract the numerators and keep the denominator, then check by adding back.
reading: A water bottle is marked in tenths. It is 7/10 full. Lena drinks 3/10 of the bottle on her walk to school. How much is left? Seven tenths take away three tenths leaves four tenths: 7/10 − 3/10 = 4/10. The *difference* is 4/10, which is the same as 2/5. Like addition, you work only with the numerators.

Sometimes you subtract from a whole. A pan of brownies is full, and someone eats 3/8 of it. To subtract, *rename* the whole 1 as 8/8, since 8 eighths fill the pan. Then 8/8 − 3/8 = 5/8 of the pan remains. Renaming 1 as a fraction with the right denominator makes the subtraction easy.

Two mistakes show up often. One is subtracting the denominators as well, which gives a denominator of 0 and makes no sense. Another is forgetting to rename 1. Always check by adding back. If 1 − 3/8 = 5/8, then 5/8 + 3/8 should be 8/8, which is 1. It is, so the answer is right.

words.d: the answer to a subtraction problem; the difference of 7/10 and 3/10 is 4/10
to write a number as an equivalent fraction, like writing 1 as 8/8

look.title: A Bottle Marked in Tenths
look.cite: an example bottle with 10 equal marks
look.prompt: Check each row by subtracting. How much of the bottle did Lena drink in all? Write the amount left at the end as a fraction.

check.why: 9 − 4 = 5 twelfths. The denominator stays 12, so the difference is 5/12.

check.q: Which addition checks that 8/9 − 5/9 = 3/9 is correct?
check.why: Adding the answer back to what was taken away should give the start: 3/9 + 5/9 = 8/9. It does.

lessons.title: Mixed Numbers With Like Denominators
lessons.mainIdea: Add or subtract the whole parts and the fraction parts separately, then regroup any fraction that is more than one.
reading: A carpenter joins two boards end to end: one is 2 3/4 feet long and the other is 1 2/4 feet. Add the wholes: 2 + 1 = 3. Add the fractions: 3/4 + 2/4 = 5/4. But 5/4 is more than one whole, so *regroup* it as 1 1/4. Now add that 1 to the 3 wholes: 3 + 1 1/4 = 4 1/4 feet.

Subtraction can need regrouping the other way. Try 3 1/4 − 1 3/4. You cannot take 3/4 from 1/4. So *rename* 3 1/4 by borrowing one whole: 3 1/4 = 2 + 4/4 + 1/4 = 2 5/4. Now subtract: 2 5/4 − 1 3/4 = 1 2/4, which is 1 1/2. Another route is to turn both into fourths: 13/4 − 7/4 = 6/4 = 1 1/2. Same answer.

The common mistake is to subtract the smaller fraction from the bigger one no matter where it sits: 3/4 − 1/4 = 2/4, giving 2 2/4. That is wrong. Check by adding: 1 3/4 + 2 2/4 = 4 1/4, not 3 1/4. The true answer 1 1/2 checks: 1 3/4 + 1 2/4 = 2 5/4 = 3 1/4.

words.d: to trade pieces for a whole, or a whole for pieces, like turning 5/4 into 1 1/4
to write a number a different way without changing its value, like 3 1/4 = 2 5/4

look.title: Two Boards on the Bench
look.text: One board is 2 5/8 feet long and another is 1 7/8 feet. Placed end to end, the wholes give 3 feet and the eighths give 5/8 + 7/8 = 12/8. Since 8/8 is one foot, 12/8 = 1 4/8, and the total is 4 4/8, or 4 1/2 feet. Now a 4 1/8-foot board needs a 2 5/8-foot piece cut off.
look.prompt: Rename 4 1/8 so you can subtract 2 5/8 from it. How long is the piece that is left? Check your answer by adding it to 2 5/8.

check.q: To subtract 5 1/6 − 2 5/6, how should you rename 5 1/6 first?
check.why: Borrow one whole as 6/6: 5 1/6 = 4 + 6/6 + 1/6 = 4 7/6. Now 7/6 − 5/6 works.

lessons.title: Finding a Common Denominator
lessons.mainIdea: To add or subtract fractions with different denominators, first rename them so they share the same denominator.
reading: Try 1/2 + 1/3. Halves and thirds are different sizes, so you cannot just count them. You need pieces that fit both. A *common denominator* is a number that both denominators divide into. For 2 and 3, that number is 6. Rename: 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6. Now both fractions are sixths, and you can add.

How do you find one? List the *multiples* of each denominator. Multiples of 2: 2, 4, 6, 8. Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9. The first number on both lists is 6. For 4 and 6, the multiples are 4, 8, 12 and 6, 12, so 12 works. Multiplying the denominators, 4 × 6 = 24, also works, but 12 is smaller and easier.

Often one denominator already divides the other. For 3/4 + 1/8, use 8. Rename 3/4 as 6/8, and leave 1/8 alone. The big mistake is changing only the denominator: writing 1/2 as 1/6. That shrinks the amount. Whatever you multiply the bottom by, multiply the top by the same number.

words.d: a denominator shared by two or more fractions after renaming, like 6 for 1/2 and 1/3
a number you get by multiplying; 6, 12 and 18 are multiples of 6

look.title: Multiples of 4 and 6
look.prompt: What is the smallest number that appears in both lists? Use it to rename 3/4 and 5/6 with the same denominator.

check.q: What is a common denominator for 1/3 and 1/4?
check.why: Multiples of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12. Both lists reach 12, so 12 is a common denominator.
3 × 4 = 12, so multiply the top by 4 too: 2 × 4 = 8. 2/3 = 8/12.

check.q: What is the smallest common denominator for 5/6 and 1/4?
check.why: Multiples of 6: 6, 12. Multiples of 4: 4, 8, 12. The smallest shared multiple is 12. 24 also works but is not the smallest.

lessons.title: Adding Unlike Fractions
lessons.mainIdea: Rename the fractions with a common denominator, then add the numerators and keep that denominator.
reading: Priya walks 1/2 mile to the library and then 1/3 mile to the park. How far did she walk? The fractions have *unlike denominators*, so rename them in sixths: 1/2 = 3/6 and 1/3 = 2/6. Now add: 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. She walked 5/6 of a mile.

Try one that passes a whole. A recipe needs 3/4 cup of flour for the batter and 5/8 cup for the topping. Use eighths: 3/4 = 6/8. Then 6/8 + 5/8 = 11/8. Eight eighths make 1 cup, and 3/8 is left, so the recipe needs 1 3/8 cups of flour in all.

The common mistake is adding across: 1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5. You can catch it with an *estimate*. 1/2 plus a little more must be more than 1/2. But 2/5 is less than 1/2, since half of 5 is 2 1/2. So 2/5 cannot be the sum. Estimating first tells you what size answer to expect.

words.d: different denominators in two fractions, like 1/2 and 1/3
a quick, rough answer used to check whether an exact answer makes sense

look.title: Two Walks in One Afternoon
look.text: Diego walks 2/3 mile to a friend's house and then 1/4 mile to the store. To add, he renames both in twelfths: 2/3 = 8/12 and 1/4 = 3/12, so the total is 11/12 mile. On the way home he walks 3/5 mile and then 1/2 mile.
look.prompt: Rename 3/5 and 1/2 with a common denominator and add them. Is the answer more than 1 mile? Estimate first, then compute.

check.why: Rename in twelfths: 1/4 = 3/12 and 2/3 = 8/12. Then 3/12 + 8/12 = 11/12.
1/2 = 4/8, so 4/8 + 3/8 = 7/8. The denominator stays 8.
1/2 = 3/6, so 5/6 + 3/6 = 8/6. That is 1 whole and 2/6, which is 1 1/3.

lessons.title: Subtracting Unlike Fractions
lessons.mainIdea: Rename with a common denominator, subtract the numerators, and check that the answer is reasonable.
reading: A ribbon is 3/4 yard long. Nia cuts off 1/3 yard for a bow. How much is left? Fourths and thirds need a common denominator, and 12 works. Rename: 3/4 = 9/12 and 1/3 = 4/12. Subtract: 9/12 − 4/12 = 5/12. There is 5/12 yard of ribbon left.

Mixed numbers work the same way. Take 2 1/2 − 3/4. Rename in fourths: 2 1/2 = 2 2/4. You cannot take 3/4 from 2/4, so borrow: 2 2/4 = 1 6/4. Now 1 6/4 − 3/4 = 1 3/4. Or write 2 1/2 as 5/2 = 10/4, and 10/4 − 3/4 = 7/4 = 1 3/4. Both roads reach 1 3/4.

Always *check by adding*: 5/12 + 4/12 = 9/12 = 3/4, so the ribbon answer is right. Ask whether the answer is *reasonable*. Since 1/3 is more than 1/4, taking 1/3 from 3/4 must leave less than 1/2. 5/12 is less than 6/12, so it fits. The usual mistakes are subtracting denominators, or renaming the bottom but not the top.

words.d: to test a subtraction answer by adding it back to the amount you took away
close to what an estimate says the answer should be

look.title: Leftover Paint
look.text: A can holds 7/8 gallon of paint. Owen uses 1/4 gallon on a bookshelf. He renames 1/4 as 2/8 and subtracts: 7/8 − 2/8 = 5/8 gallon left. The next day he starts with 2/3 gallon in a second can and uses 1/2 gallon.
look.prompt: Find a common denominator for 2/3 and 1/2, and subtract. How much paint is left in the second can? Check by adding your answer to 1/2.

check.why: 1/3 = 2/6, so 5/6 − 2/6 = 3/6, which is 1/2. The choice 2/3 comes from subtracting 5 − 1 without renaming.

lessons.title: A Fraction Times a Whole Number
lessons.mainIdea: Multiplying a fraction by a whole number is repeated addition: 3 × 2/5 means three jumps of 2/5, which is 6/5.
reading: Each day Sofia runs 2/5 of a mile. In 3 days she runs 3 × 2/5. That is 2/5 + 2/5 + 2/5, three jumps of 2/5 on a number line. Count the fifths: 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 fifths, so the *product* is 6/5, which is 1 1/5 miles. The rule: multiply the numerator by the whole number and keep the denominator.

The word *of* also means multiply. Suppose 2/5 of a class of 15 students ride the bus. Split 15 into 5 equal groups: 15 ÷ 5 = 3 students in each fifth. Two fifths are 2 × 3 = 6 students. The rule gives the same answer: 2/5 × 15 = 30/5 = 6.

A common mistake is multiplying both the top and the bottom: 3 × 2/5 = 6/15. But 6/15 equals 2/5, so nothing got bigger. Only the numerator is multiplied. Try 4 × 3/4. That is 12/4, and 12 fourths make exactly 3 wholes. Four servings of 3/4 cup is 3 cups.

words.d: the answer to a multiplication problem; the product of 3 and 2/5 is 6/5
in math, a word that means multiply, as in 2/5 of 15 = 2/5 × 15

look.title: Walking 3/4 Mile Each Day
look.cite: each row is 3/4 multiplied by the number of days
look.prompt: Write each row as a fraction with denominator 4. After 4 days, how many whole miles is that? After 5 days, write the distance as a mixed number.

check.why: 4 × 2 = 8 thirds, or 8/3. Six thirds make 2, and 2/3 is left, so 8/3 = 2 2/3.
One fourth of 20 is 20 ÷ 4 = 5. Three fourths are 3 × 5 = 15. Also 3/4 × 20 = 60/4 = 15.
5 × 3 = 15 tenths, or 15/10. Ten tenths make 1, and 5/10 = 1/2 is left, so the product is 1 1/2.

lessons.title: A Fraction Times a Fraction
lessons.mainIdea: To multiply two fractions, multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators; an area model shows why.
reading: What is 1/2 of 3/4 of a brownie pan? Draw the pan as a rectangle. Cut it into 4 columns and shade 3 of them for 3/4. Now cut the pan into 2 rows and take the top row for 1/2. The part shaded both ways is 3 small pieces out of 8 in the whole pan. So 1/2 × 3/4 = 3/8. This picture is an *area model*.

The model gives a rule. The rows times the columns give the total pieces, so denominators multiply: 2 × 4 = 8. The shaded rows times the shaded columns give the double-shaded pieces, so numerators multiply: 1 × 3 = 3. Try 2/3 × 4/5. Numerators: 2 × 4 = 8. Denominators: 3 × 5 = 15. The product is 8/15.

Some students look for a common denominator before multiplying. You do not need one; each *factor* keeps its own denominator. Also, simplify at the end when you can. 2/3 × 3/4 = 6/12, and 6/12 = 1/2. A quick check: half of 3/4 should be a bit less than half of 1, and 3/8 is a bit less than 4/8. It fits.

words.d: a rectangle cut into rows and columns that shows a fraction of a fraction
a number being multiplied; in 2/3 × 4/5 the factors are 2/3 and 4/5

look.title: The Community Garden Plot
look.text: A garden plot in a Chicago neighborhood is one whole rectangle. Vegetables take up 2/5 of it. Half of the vegetable part is tomatoes. Draw the plot with 5 columns, shade 2 for vegetables, then cut it into 2 rows and take 1 row. The tomatoes cover 2 of the 10 small pieces, so 1/2 × 2/5 = 2/10 = 1/5 of the plot.
look.prompt: Now use an area model for 3/4 × 2/3. How many small pieces are in the whole, and how many are shaded twice? Write the product in simplest form.

check.why: Numerators: 1 × 3 = 3. Denominators: 3 × 5 = 15. So the product is 3/15, which simplifies to 1/5.
2 × 5 = 10 and 3 × 6 = 18, so the product is 10/18. Divide both by 2: 5/9.

check.q: An area model has 4 rows and 5 columns. The shaded part covers 2 rows and 3 columns. Which product does it show?
check.why: 2/4 × 3/5: the whole has 4 × 5 = 20 pieces, and 2 × 3 = 6 are shaded twice. The product is 6/20, or 3/10.

lessons.title: Bigger or Smaller? Scaling
lessons.mainIdea: Multiplying by a fraction less than 1 makes a number smaller; multiplying by a number greater than 1 makes it bigger.
reading: Multiplying does not always make things bigger. Start with 8. Multiply by 1/2 and you get 4, which is smaller. Multiply by 3/2 and you get 24/2 = 12, which is bigger. Multiply by 1 and you get 8, the same. Multiplying by a number is *scaling*: the factor tells you whether the result grows, shrinks or stays put.

You can predict the size before you compute. 3/4 × 2/3 must be less than 2/3, because 3/4 is *less than 1*. And 5/4 × 2/3 must be more than 2/3, because 5/4 is more than 1. Check: 3/4 × 2/3 = 6/12 = 1/2, which is less than 2/3. Then 5/4 × 2/3 = 10/12 = 5/6, which is more than 2/3.

The common mistake is to assume a product is always larger than both factors. That is true for whole numbers bigger than 1, but not for fractions. If you eat 2/3 of a 12-inch sub, you eat 2/3 × 12 = 8 inches, less than the whole sub. When one factor is less than 1, expect the answer to be smaller than the other factor.

words.d: multiplying a number to make it bigger or smaller by a certain factor
a number between 0 and 1, like 3/4; multiplying by it shrinks a number

look.title: Scaling the Number 8
look.cite: each product computed from 8 times the factor
look.prompt: Which factors made the product smaller than 8, and what do those factors have in common? Predict 8 × 5/4 without computing, then check it.

check.q: Without computing, what can you say about 7/8 × 5?
check.why: 7/8 is less than 1, so multiplying 5 by it gives less than 5. In fact 7/8 × 5 = 35/8 = 4 3/8.
Only 4/3 is greater than 1, so only 4/3 × 2/3 = 8/9 is more than 2/3. The others shrink 2/3 or leave it the same.
12 × 3 = 36 halves, and 36/2 = 18. Since 3/2 is more than 1, the answer is bigger than 12.

lessons.title: Recipes and Measurements
lessons.mainIdea: Read the problem, decide whether to add, subtract or multiply, compute carefully, and then ask whether the answer makes sense.
reading: A cookie recipe uses 2/3 cup of sugar. Making three batches means 3 × 2/3 = 6/3 = 2 cups of sugar. Making half a batch means 1/2 × 2/3 = 2/6 = 1/3 cup. In a *word problem*, "three batches" and "half a batch" both mean multiply. Ask what is being scaled and by how much.

Measurements often need adding. A 5/8-inch board is glued on top of a 3/4-inch board. The total thickness is 5/8 + 3/4. Rename 3/4 as 6/8: 5/8 + 6/8 = 11/8 = 1 3/8 inches. Cutting a piece off means subtracting. Combining pieces means adding. Making copies means multiplying.

The most common mistake is picking the operation from a single word instead of the situation. "Half" can mean multiply by 1/2 or subtract 1/2, depending on the story. After computing, check that the answer is *reasonable*: two batches need more sugar, not less; a glued stack is thicker than either board alone.

words.d: a math problem told as a story that you have to turn into numbers and operations
an answer that is the right size for the story it comes from

look.title: Trail Mix for the Hike
look.text: Kai mixes 3/4 cup of peanuts, 1/2 cup of raisins and 1/3 cup of chocolate chips. He renames everything in twelfths: 9/12 + 6/12 + 4/12 = 19/12, which is 1 7/12 cups in all. His friend wants only half a batch.
look.prompt: How many cups of peanuts go in half a batch? How much trail mix does half a batch make? Which operation did you use each time, and why?

check.q: A recipe calls for 3/4 cup of milk. How much milk is needed for a double recipe?
check.why: 2 × 3/4 = 6/4. Four fourths make 1 cup, and 2/4 = 1/2 is left, so 1 1/2 cups.

check.q: A rope is 2 1/2 feet long. You cut off 3/4 foot. How much rope is left?
A serving is 3/4 cup. How much is 1/3 of a serving?
check.why: 1/3 × 3/4 = 3/12, which is 1/4 cup. Check: three 1/4 cups make 3/4 cup.

review.why: 4 + 2 = 6 ninths, or 6/9. Divide top and bottom by 3: 2/3.
5/6 is less than 1, so 3/4 × 5/6 = 15/24 = 5/8 is smaller than 3/4. The other factors are 1 or more.

review.q: A recipe uses 1/4 cup of oil. How much oil is needed for 5 batches?
review.why: 5 × 1/4 = 5/4. Four fourths make 1 cup, and 1/4 is left, so 1 1/4 cups.
